Normalisation is a step-by-step process for structuring data into well-designed relations. It minimises redundancy and so prevents update, insertion and deletion anomalies. An update anomaly occurs when the same fact stored in several rows is changed in some but not all of them.
Makes sense. Keep going.
An insertion anomaly is being unable to add data because other unrelated data is missing. A deletion anomaly is losing useful data when another record is removed.
Right. What else do we need to know?

First normal form removes repeating groups so each field holds a single atomic value; the repeating group goes into a new table carrying the original key, which becomes part of a composite key. Second normal form removes partial dependencies, where a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite key.
Got it. Keep going.

Third normal form removes transitive dependencies, where a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute. A relation with a single-attribute key in first normal form is automatically in second normal form.

Normalisation?
A formal process of organising data into relations to minimise redundancy and prevent update, insertion and deletion anomalies.
First normal form (first normal form)?
A relation with no repeating groups in which every attribute holds a single atomic value.
Second normal form (second normal form)?
A relation in first normal form with no partial dependencies on a composite key.
Third normal form (third normal form)?
A relation in second normal form with no transitive dependencies, so every non-key attribute depends only on the primary key.
Partial dependency?
Where a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite primary key.
Transitive dependency?
Where a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute rather than directly on the primary key.
